items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 7 "Describe": Why is it important for scientists around the world to define the second in the same way?

answer.html: A common definition means that a time measured in one laboratory means exactly the same thing in every other laboratory. Results can then be compared, repeated, and trusted. If each country used its own "second," experiments that depend on timing (such as GPS satellite signals) could not be shared or checked.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: A unit is used by labs worldwide.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Comparable result = same unit definition everywhere.

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: 1 s in lab A = 1 s in lab B only if both use the same standard.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: A common definition means that a time measured in one laboratory means exactly the same thing in every other laboratory. Results can then be compared, repeated, and trusted. If each country used its own "second," experiments that depend on timing (such as GPS satellite signals) could not be shared or checked.

items.title: Lesson 2, "Get It?" (page 11): A new hard drive can store 4,000,000,000,000 bytes. What metric prefix describes this amount?

body.html: From Table 2, the prefix for 10<sup>12</sup> is tera- (T).
4, 000, 000, 000, 000 = 4 × 10<sup>12</sup>, so the drive stores 4 terabytes.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 8 "Infer": A graduated cylinder is marked every 1 mL, and the liquid level reads 24.3 mL. Why is the last digit uncertain?

answer.html: The first two digits (24) come from marks you can read directly. The last digit (0.1 mL) is an estimate of where the liquid surface falls between two marks, so different people might estimate 24.2, 24.3, or 24.4 mL. That estimated digit is the uncertain one.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: Marks every 1 mL; reading 24.3 mL.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Last recorded digit = estimate between the finest marks.

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: 24 mL read from marks; 0.3 mL estimated between 24 mL and 25 mL.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: The first two digits (24) come from marks you can read directly. The last digit (0.1 mL) is an estimate of where the liquid surface falls between two marks, so different people might estimate 24.2, 24.3, or 24.4 mL. That estimated digit is the uncertain one.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 7: Why do engineers describe how a beam bends with a formula instead of only in words?

answer.html: A formula states an exact relationship between measurable quantities, such as load, length, and bending. It lets engineers make numerical predictions, test them against measurements, and communicate the idea without any ambiguity, which a verbal description cannot do.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: A beam bends under a load.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Formula: bending = f(load, length, material).

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: Plug in a load in N and length in m to predict the bend in m.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: A formula states an exact relationship between measurable quantities, such as load, length, and bending. It lets engineers make numerical predictions, test them against measurements, and communicate the idea without any ambiguity, which a verbal description cannot do.

body.html: For subtraction, round to the least precise decimal place. 15.7 has one decimal place.
15.7 −9.318 = 6.382, rounded to one decimal place.
8.62 −0.5271 = 8.0929. The less precise number (8.62) has two decimal places.
For multiplication, keep the fewest significant figures. 3.4 has 2.
212 × 3.4 = 720.8, rounded to 2 significant figures.
17.92 / 14.6 = 1.2274; 14.6 has three significant figures.
Convert to the same unit first, then add and round to the least precise term.
2.3 km = 2300 m (precise only to 0.1 km = 100 m). 850 cm = 8.50 m.
The least precise term, 2.3 km, is known only to the nearest 0.1 km, so the sum is rounded to the nearest 0.1 km.

The smaller terms do not change the first two digits.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 11: A bicycle computer shows that a rider traveled at 85 km/h along a flat, level road. Is this reasonable?

body.html: Compare with everyday experience by converting to familiar units.
That is about 53 mi/h, faster than any ordinary rider can pedal on level ground (typical riders are about 20–30 km/h).

answer.html: Not reasonable for a rider on a flat road, so the reading probably comes from an error (a wrong wheel-size setting or a sensor problem). It could be reasonable for a professional sprinter drafting behind a vehicle, or for a rider coasting down a long steep hill.

check.html: 24 m/s is about highway car speed, which is far beyond ordinary pedaling.

items.title: Lesson 2, Figure 7 "Describe": Why is it important to have standards for measurements?

answer.html: Standards give everyone the same reference for each unit, so measurements made by different people in different places can be compared, repeated, and trusted. Without a common standard (for example, everyone's own "step" as a meter), results could not be shared or checked.

stepCards.label: Givens
stepCards.html: Measurements are made by many people in many places.

stepCards.label: Equation
stepCards.html: Comparable result = same unit standard everywhere.

stepCards.label: Substitute
stepCards.html: 1 m measured anywhere means the same length only with a shared standard.

stepCards.label: Answer
stepCards.html: Standards give everyone the same reference for each unit, so measurements made by different people in different places can be compared, repeated, and trusted. Without a common standard (for example, everyone's own "step" as a meter), results could not be shared or checked.

items.title: Check Your Progress, Problem 11: Is 290 km/h reasonable for a car's speed?

body.html: Compare to everyday experience. Convert the speed to familiar units.
That is about 180 mi/h, far faster than highway speed limits (about 100–130 km/h).

answer.html: Not reasonable for an ordinary car, which suggests an error in the values or setup (for example, a wrong time or distance, or a unit mix-up). It could be reasonable for a special case such as a race car on a track (Formula 1 or other high-performance racers) or a high-speed train or other vehicle designed to travel that fast.

check.html: 81 m/s is about the take-off speed of an airliner, which shows how fast that is for a road vehicle.
